These are the five planets (al-kawakib al-darariyy): Zuhal (Saturn), al-Mushtari (Jupiter), 'Utarid (Mercury), al-Mirrikh (Mars), and al-Zuhra (Venus), according to what the people of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) have mentioned. And God knows best. This is also narrated from 'Ali, may God honour his face. There are two views on why these are singled out from among the other stars. The first: because they face the sun. This was said by Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah al-Muzani. The second: because they cross the Milky Way (al-Majarra). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: they are the stars that recede by day and when they set. 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, also said this, and said: they are the stars that recede by day and appear by night, and that they hide (takannas) at the time of their setting, meaning they withdraw from sight because of their obscurity, so they are not seen.

In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari): "bi-l-khunnas" refers to all the stars, because they recede at setting, or because they recede by day. It is also said that among the stars, it refers to the wandering ones (al-sayyara) and not the fixed ones. Al-Farra' said regarding God's words, ﴿So I swear not by the stars that recede, that run and hide﴾: they are the five stars, Zuhal, al-Mushtari, al-Mirrikh, al-Zuhra and 'Utarid, because they recede in their orbit and hide, as gazelles hide in caves (al-maghar), and that is the kinnas (hiding place). It is also said they were called khunnas because of their lagging behind, since they are the wandering stars which retrograde and then go direct. It is said: "khanasa 'anhu yakhnusu bi-d-damm khunusan," meaning he lagged behind; and "akhnasahu ghayruhu" means when someone left him behind and went on away from him. The khans is the nose receding from the face with a slight elevation at the tip, and the man is akhnas, the woman khansa', and cattle are all khuns.

It has been narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud regarding His words, ﴿So I swear not by the khunnas﴾, that they are wild cattle (baqar al-wahsh). Hushaym narrated from Zakariyya, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu Maysara 'Amr ibn Shurahbil, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said to me: "You are an Arab people, so what are the khunnas?" I said: "They are wild cattle." He said: "I also think so." Ibrahim and Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah also said this. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "God only swore by wild cattle." And 'Ikrima narrated from him, saying: "By the khunnas: the cattle, and the kunnas: they are the gazelles; they are khunnas when they see a person, they recede, withdraw, lag behind and enter their kinas (hiding place)."

Al-Qushayri said: It is also said on this view that "bi-l-khunnas" comes from "al-khanas" in the nose, which is the receding of the tip and shortness of the bridge, and the noses of cattle and gazelles are khunnas. The more sound view is to interpret it as referring to the stars, because the night and dawn are mentioned after this, so mention of the stars is more fitting for that.

I say: God may swear by whatever He wills of His creatures, whether animate or inanimate, even if the wisdom behind that is not known. It has come from Ibn Mas'ud, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah (both of them Companions), and al-Nakha'i that they are wild cattle. And from Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr that they are gazelles. And from al-Hajjaj ibn al-Mundhir, who said: "I asked Jabir ibn Zayd about al-jawari al-kunnas, and he said: the gazelles and the cattle." So it is not far-fetched that the intended meaning is the stars. It has also been said that they are the angels, as al-Mawardi related.

Al-kunnas means the hidden ones, derived from al-kinas, which is the hiding place of wild animals where they conceal themselves. Aws ibn Hajar said:

"Have you not seen that God sent down His rain,
and the gazelles in their kinas were being stung by gnats (tuqammi')?" [[Taqma': they move their heads from the stinging of the qam'a, a blue fly that enters the noses of animals or settles on them and stings them.]]

And Tarafa said:

"As if the two kinas of a sidr tree (dalla) enclose it,
and the bends of bows beneath a strong, supported spine." [[He said "two kinas" because the animal hides in its shade in the morning and in its shelter in the evening. The dalla is the wild jujube, singular dalla. The atr is the bend. The mu'ayyad is the strengthened. The poet says: "As if the two kinas of a dalla tree enclose this she-camel's ... ..." between her forearms and her chest.]]

It is also said: al-kunus means to take refuge in their makasis, which are the places where the wild animals and gazelles take shelter. Al-A'sha said:

"When we came to the tribe, Anas raised his neck,
as the gazelle raised its neck beneath the makasis, the female antelope."

It is said: "tala'a" means the day rose high, and the gazelle "atla'at" from its kinas, meaning she raised her neck. And Imru' al-Qays said:

"He grazed a little, then turned his hooves [[Ta'shsha: entered the evening, which is the beginning of the night. Zulufuhu: its hooves.]],
stirring up dust from a resting place and a den."

Al-kunns is the plural of kanis and kanisa, and likewise al-khunns is the plural of khanis and khanisa. Al-jawari is the plural of jariya, from jara yajri.

(And by the night when it turns away.) Al-Farra' said: the mufassirun agreed that the meaning of "'asm'asa" is "adbara" (it turned away), related by al-Jawhari. Some of our companions said: it means it drew near at its beginning and became dark, just as a cloud draws near the earth. Al-Mahdawi said: "wa-l-layli idha 'as'asa" means it turned away with its darkness, from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others. It is also narrated from them, and from al-Hasan and others, that it "approached" with its darkness. Zayd ibn Aslam said: "'as'asa" means it departed. Al-Farra' said: the Arabs say "as'asa" and "sa'sa'a" when only a little of it remains. Al-Khalil and others said: the night "as'asa" when it approached or when it turned away. Al-Mubarrad said: it is one of the words with contradictory meanings (al-adداd), and both meanings return to one thing, which is the beginning of darkness at its start and its turning away at its end. 'Alqama ibn Qurt said:

"Until, when the dawn breathed for it,
and its night was cleared away and 'as'asa."

And Ru'ba said:

"O Hind, how quickly he 'tasa'sa'a'
after he had been a tender, delicate youth." [[Tas'sa'a: turned away and perished. The sar'ara: the young, soft man.]]

This is the proof of al-Farra'. And Imru' al-Qays said [[So it is in all the originals and we did not find it in his diwan. In Lisan: "kana lahu min daw'ihi miqbas." Then it says: Abu al-Buldan the grammarian recited it and said: they used to consider this verse fabricated. And our original text is: "idh dana" (when it drew near), then assimilated.]]:

"It 'as'asa until, if it wished, it drew near,
there would be for us a flame from its fire as a firebrand."

This indicates approach. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: "as'asa" means it became dark. The poet said:

"Until, when their night 'as'asa for them,
they rode from the edge of darkness, a dark night."

Al-Mawardi said: the root of "al-'ass" is fullness, and from this the large cup is called "'ass" because it is full of what is in it. So it is applied to the night's approach at the beginning of its fullness, and it is applied to its turning away at the end of its fullness with its darkness, for the completion of its fullness with it. As for the words of Imru' al-Qays:

"Alamma 'ala al-rab' al-qadim bi-'as'asa [[Its completion: 'As though I were called, or hills silent.']]"

this is a place in the desert. "'As'asa" is also the name of a man. The rajiz said: "wa-'as'asa ni'ma al-fata tabayyahu," meaning he relies on him. The wolf is called al-'as'as, al-'as'as and al-'assas, because it prowls at night and seeks. Hedgehogs are called al-'asa'is because of their frequent movement at night. Abu 'Amr said: al-ta'as'us is sniffing, and he recited: "Like the nostril of a wolf when it sniffs (ta'as'asa)." And al-ta'as'us is also: seeking game [at night [[The addition is from al-Sihah.]]].

(And by the dawn when it breathes.) That is, it extended until it became clear daylight. It is said of the day when it increases: "tanaffasa." Likewise the wave when it sprinkles water. The meaning of "tanaffus" is the emergence of breeze from within. It is also said: "idha tanaffasa" means it split and cracked, and from this comes "tanaffasat al-qaws," meaning it cracked. [[In the original manuscripts: "tanaffasat al-qaws wa-l-nufus" (the bow and the souls were split). The lexicon makes no mention of the word "al-nufus," and perhaps it is an addition by the copyist.]]

(Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger.) This is the answer to the oath. The noble messenger is Jibril (Gabriel), said by al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Dahhak. The meaning: it is indeed the word of a noble messenger from God, noble before God. He attributed the speech to Jibril, peace be upon him, and then removed it from him by saying: ﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Waqi'a 56:80], so that those of verification in belief would know that the speech belongs to God, Mighty and Majestic. It is also said: it is Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. (Possessor of power.) For whoever takes it to be Jibril, his power is evident. Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "From his power is that he uprooted the cities of the people of Lut with the tips of his wing feathers."

(Honoured in the presence of the Lord of the Throne.) That is, in the presence of God, may His praise be exalted, (of high rank.) That is, possessor of station and standing. It is narrated from Abu Salih, who said: "He enters seventy veils without permission."

(Obeyed there, trustworthy.) That is, in the heavens. Ibn 'Abbas said: from the obedience of the angels to Jibril: when the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, was taken on the Night Journey, Jibril, peace be upon him, said to Ridwan, the keeper of the Gardens: "Open it for him." He opened, and he entered and saw what was in it. And he said to Malik, the keeper of the Fire: "Open Jahannam for him so that he may look at it." He obeyed him and opened it for him.

(Trustworthy.) That is, entrusted with the revelation he brings. And whoever says the intended one is Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, then the meaning is: possessor of power to convey the message, obeyed, that is, whoever obeys God, Mighty and Majestic, obeys him.

(And your companion is not mad.) He means Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, is not mad so that he could be accused regarding his words. This is part of the answer to the oath. It is also said: the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, wished to see Jibril in the form in which he is with his Lord, Mighty and Majestic. He said: "That is not up to me." So the Lord, may His praise be exalted, permitted him, and he came to him having filled the horizon. When the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, looked at him, he fell down unconscious. The polytheists said: "He is mad." So this was revealed: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, and your companion is not mad﴾. He had seen Jibril in his true form, and was awed by him, and what his structure could not bear came upon him, so he fell down unconscious.

**Verse 23: ﴿And he certainly saw him at the clear horizon﴾**, that is, Jibril saw him in his true form, and he had six hundred wings. **"At the clear horizon"** means at the place where the sun rises from the east, because when the sun rises from this horizon it is "clear" (mubin), meaning that things are seen from its direction. It has also been said that the clear horizon means the regions and quarters of the sky. A poet said:

*We took the horizons of the sky over you,*
*for us are its two moons and the rising stars.*

Al-Mawardi said: On this view there are three opinions. The first is that he saw him on the eastern horizon of the sky; this was said by Sufyan. The second is that he saw him on the western horizon of the sky; this was related by Ibn Shajarah. The third is that he saw him toward Ajyad, which is the eastern side of Makkah; this was said by Mujahid. Al-Tha'labi related from Ibn Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Jibril: "I love to see you in your form in which you are in the sky." He said: "You will not be able to do that." He said: "Yes." He said: "Where do you wish that I should appear to you?" He said: "In al-Abtah." He said: "It cannot contain me." He said: "Then in Mina." He said: "It cannot contain me." He said: "Then in 'Arafat." He said: "That is more fitting for it to contain me." So the Prophet (ﷺ) went out at once, and behold, Jibril had come with a rushing and a rumbling from the mountains of 'Arafat, filling what lies between the east and the west, his head in the sky and his feet on the earth. When the Prophet (ﷺ) saw him, he fell down unconscious. Jibril changed into human form, embraced him to his chest, and said: "O Muhammad, do not fear. How would you be if you saw Israfil, whose head is beneath the Throne and whose feet are in the depths of the seventh earth? The Throne is on his shoulder, and at times he shrinks out of fear of Allah until he becomes like the wiss, meaning the sparrow, until he carries nothing of the Throne of your Lord except its greatness."

(Footnote in the source: The wiss (in *Lisan al-'Arab*, under w-s-') is the small sparrow.)

It has also been said that Muhammad (ﷺ) saw his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, at the clear horizon, and this is the meaning of the statement of Ibn Mas'ud. The discussion of this has already passed in *al-Najm* in full, so reflect on it there.

(Footnote in the source: See vol. 17, p. 94. The statement of Ibn Mas'ud there is that Muhammad (ﷺ) saw Jibril, and the one who said he saw his Lord was Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.)

Regarding **"clear" (al-mubin)** there are two views. The first is that it is an attribute of the horizon; this was said by al-Rabi'. The second is that it is an attribute of the one who saw him; this was said by Mujahid.

**Verse 24: ﴿And he is not stingy with the unseen﴾**: With the letter *ẓā'* (*ḍanīn* with ẓ, *ẓanīn*), this is the recital of Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i, meaning *not accused* (*bi-muttahamin*). *Al-Ẓinnah* is accusation. A poet said:

*By the Book of Allah and his splendour, I was not abandoned,*
*but the accused is (always) accused.*

Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading, because they did not call him stingy but called him a liar. Also, most Arabic usage says *mā huwa bi-kadhā* ("he is not such-and-such"), and they do not say *mā huwa 'alā kadhā*; they say *mā anta 'alā hādhā bi-muttahamin*.

The rest read *bi-ḍanīn* with the letter *ḍād*, meaning *stingy* (*bi-bakhīl*), from *ḍanantu bi-l-shay'* ("I was stingy with the thing"), *aḍannu ḍannan*, so he is *ḍanīn*. Ibn Abi Najīḥ related from Mujahid that he said: "He is not stingy toward you with what he knows, but teaches the creation the speech of Allah and His rulings." A poet said:

*I give generously with the hidden speech, though I am*

**Verse 25: ﴿And it is not the word of an accursed devil﴾**: (*wa-mā huwa*), meaning the Qur'an, (*bi-qawli shayṭānin rajīm*), that is, stoned and cursed, as Quraysh said. 'Ata' said: He means by the devil the white devil, who used to come to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the form of Jibril, wanting to tempt him.

**Verse 26: ﴿Then where are you going?﴾** Qatadah said: "Then to where are you turning away from this word and from obedience to it?" Thus Ma'mar related from Qatadah, meaning: where are you going away from My Book and My obedience? Al-Zajjaj said: "Then what path are you taking that is clearer than this path which I have made clear to you?" It is said: *ayna tadhhabu?* and *ila ayna tadhhabu?* ("where are you going?" and "to where are you going?"). Al-Farra' related from the Arabs: *dhahabtu al-Shām* ("I went to al-Sham"), *kharajtu al-'Irāq* ("I left Iraq"), and *inṭalaqtu al-sūq* ("I set off to the market"), meaning *ilayhā* (to it). He said: "We heard it in these three words." One of the Banu 'Uqayl recited to me:

*Ḥanīfah shouts at us when it sees us,*
*and to which land does the shouting go?*

He means *ila ayyi arḍin tadhhabu*, "to which land does it go?", so he omitted *ila* (to).

Al-Junayd said: The meaning of the verse is connected to another verse, which is His saying, ﴿And there is nothing but that its treasuries are with Us﴾ [al-Hijr: 21]. The meaning: "What path are you taking that is clearer than the path which Allah has made clear to you?" This is the meaning of al-Zajjaj's statement.

**Verse 27: ﴿It is only a reminder to the worlds﴾**, that is, an admonition and a warning. Here *in* means *mā* (not). It has also been said: Muhammad is only a reminder.

**Verse 28: ﴿For whoever among you wills to go straight﴾**, that is, to follow the truth and remain upon it. Abu Hurayrah and Sulayman ibn Musa said: When the verse ﴿For whoever among you wills to go straight﴾ was revealed, Abu Jahl said: "The matter is up to us. If we wish we will go straight, and if we wish we will not go straight." This is the position of *al-qadar*, and it is the head of the Qadariyyah (the early school denying divine predestination). So the verse was revealed: ﴿And you will not will unless Allah wills, the Lord of the worlds﴾. By this He clarified that a servant does no good except by Allah's enabling, and no evil except by His abandonment. Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, the Arabs did not will Islam until Allah willed it for them." Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "I read in seventy-some [in the Tha'labi commentary: eighty-some] books of what Allah revealed to the prophets: whoever makes for himself a share of the will (*mashī'ah*), has disbelieved." In the revelation: ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels and the dead had spoken to them, and We had gathered upon them every thing before them, they would not have believed unless Allah willed﴾ [al-An'am: 111]. And He said: ﴿And it is not for a soul to believe except by the permission of Allah﴾ [Yunus: 100]. And He said: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas: 56]. The verses on this are many, and so are the reports, and that Allah, glorified is He, guides by Islam and leads astray by disbelief, as has passed in more than one place.

**The sura is concluded, and praise be to Allah.**
